items.item: Consistency (what a read sees) and concurrency control (what a write is allowed to do) are different guarantees; strong consistency alone does not prevent a lost-write race

at.step: Which guarantee closes this gap?

items.item: A naive check-then-write pattern against an object store is not a real check, because the check and the write are two separate, non-atomic requests

at.step: Two writers, one key, no error

items.item: A precondition header is evaluated by the server at the moment of the write, which is the only way to close a check-then-write race without a separate coordination service

at.step: Which guarantee closes this gap?

items.item: There is no rename call in the S3 API or in boto3; a rename is always implemented client-side as copy_object then delete_object

at.step: One PUT is atomic; a rename never was — unless the store has a hierarchy

items.item: If-None-Match with a value of * means create-if-absent; If-Match with an ETag means update-if-unchanged — two distinct compare-and-swap primitives, not one

items.item: A catalog-free append-only commit log can be built on conditional writes alone, by writing the next sequence number's key only if it does not already exist
A lease pattern (renew only if you still hold it) is If-Match against the lease key's own current ETag, not a separate locking service

items.item: The request-rate limit is scoped to the key prefix, not the whole bucket, so one hot key or narrow prefix can throttle while the rest of a large bucket has full headroom

at.step: A hot key range throttles, even though the bucket has no limit

items.item: Spreading writes across more key prefixes is the documented fix for prefix throttling; it is a key-space design change, not a quota increase request

items.item: A table format (Iceberg, Delta, Hudi) exists specifically because a conditional write only protects one key, not a consistent, atomic view across the many keys that make up one table
